soilTypes.name: Nitisols (Red Volcanic)
soilTypes.description: Deep, well-drained red soils from volcanic parent material. Among the most fertile soils in Kenya.
improvement: Add organic matter to improve structure

soilTypes.name: Ferralsols (Laterite)
soilTypes.description: Heavily weathered soils with high iron and aluminum content. Common in warm, humid lowland areas.

soilTypes.name: Vertisols (Black Cotton)
soilTypes.description: Dark, heavy clay soils that swell when wet and crack when dry. Difficult to work but naturally fertile.
improvement: Plant in raised beds for drainage
Avoid working when very wet — forms clods
Ideal for rice paddies due to water-holding capacity

soilTypes.name: Andosols (Volcanic Ash)
soilTypes.description: Young volcanic soils found on the slopes of Mt. Kenya, Mt. Elgon, and the Aberdares. Extremely productive.
deficiencies: Prone to erosion on steep slopes

soilTypes.name: Luvisols (Brown Loams)
soilTypes.description: Well-developed soils with clay accumulation in the subsoil. Common in transitional zones between highlands and lowlands.
improvement: Deep ploughing to break subsoil pan

soilTypes.name: Arenosols (Sandy Soils)
soilTypes.description: Light, sandy soils with poor water and nutrient retention. Found in coastal and semi-arid areas.
improvement: Add clay or compost to improve water-holding

soilTypes.name: Solonchaks (Saline/Alkaline)
soilTypes.description: Salt-affected soils found around alkaline lakes and in poorly drained ASAL areas. Very challenging for agriculture.
improvement: Often better suited for pastoral/rangeland use

soilTypes.name: Acrisols (Acidic Red-Yellow)
soilTypes.description: Acidic soils with clay accumulation. Common in high-rainfall areas that have been heavily weathered.
improvement: Avoid ammonium-based fertilizers that increase acidity

notes: Soil types and distributions are based on the Kenya Soil Survey (KSS/KARI) and the FAO-UNESCO Soil Map of the World.
Most Kenyan farms have mixed soil types. Get a soil test from KALRO (KES 500–1,500 per sample) for specific nutrient recommendations.
County-level assignments are approximate. Soil type can vary within a county depending on altitude, drainage, and parent material.
Soil pH is critical: most crops prefer 5.5–7.0. Test pH before planting and amend with lime (acidic) or gypsum (alkaline) as needed.
For personalized soil management advice, contact your county agricultural extension officer or visit the nearest KALRO research station.
